name: Kilimanjaro — Machame
tagline: Machame Gate to Uhuru Peak. Five climate zones, one mountain.

cairns.title: Machame Gate
cairns.body: The road ends here. Below the park boundary the slopes are farmland — coffee, bananas, maize — watered by streams running off the forest above. Everything that goes up the mountain from this point is carried on foot. Around 35,000 people attempt the summit each year, and with roughly four porters and guides to every climber, several hundred set out from gates like this one every morning.

cairns.title: The Rain Forest Belt
cairns.body: Kilimanjaro makes its own weather: moist air off the plains rises against the slope and drops roughly 1,800 mm of rain a year in this band — more than three times what falls on the farmland below. Camphor, podocarpus and fig dominate the wet sections, juniper and olive the drier ones, with vines, ferns and Old Man's Beard hanging through it.

cairns.title: Blue Monkey
cairns.body: Not actually blue — grey with a dark cap, and easier to hear than see. Blue monkeys and black-and-white colobus both live in this forest, along with a long list of birds. Above the treeline almost none of it follows: by the summit, apart from lichens and the odd spider, effectively nothing lives.

cairns.title: Machame Camp
cairns.body: The first camp sits right where the forest gives out. The change is abrupt rather than gradual — dense canopy one minute, open heath the next. You have climbed nearly 1,200 vertical metres from the gate, most of it under cloud.

cairns.title: Heath & Moorland
cairns.body: Grasses, proteas and giant heathers, with rainfall dropping to about 1,600 mm. Higher up, where water collects, the strangest plants on the mountain appear: giant groundsels and lobelias, which look less like alpine flora than something left behind by another era.

cairns.title: Shira Plateau
cairns.body: You are standing inside a volcano that no longer exists. Shira was the oldest of Kilimanjaro's three centres, active roughly 2.5 to 1.9 million years ago. When its eruptions ended, the cone collapsed into an enormous caldera; what's left is this broad plateau, walled on its western side by the curved remains of the rim. Boulders of porphyry lie scattered across it, some three metres across, furred with pale lichen.

cairns.title: Lava Tower
cairns.body: A volcanic plug standing clear of the slope, its base the highest point on this side of the mountain until Barafu. The rock is green and fissile with a chloritic sheen and obsidian fragments scattered through it, weathered at the foot into big angular blocks. Most groups eat lunch here and then descend — climb high, sleep low.

cairns.title: Giant Groundsel
cairns.body: A thick trunk topped with a rosette of cabbage-like leaves, several metres tall, found here and almost nowhere else. It survives nights below freezing by keeping its dead leaves wrapped around the trunk as insulation and folding the living rosette shut over its growing bud.

cairns.title: Barranco Wall
cairns.body: About 100,000 years ago a vast landslip breached the southern crater wall and carried away something like 1,000 metres of the cone. The valley you camp in, and the wall you climb out of it in the morning, are the scar. Lava flows are exposed in cross-section across its face.

cairns.title: Thin Air
cairns.body: Roughly a third of climbers don't summit, and altitude is the main reason — not fitness. This is why the route deliberately climbs to Lava Tower and then drops back down, and why guides repeat pole pole, slowly slowly. The alpine desert around you receives about 250 mm of rain a year; the summit gets half that.

cairns.title: Barafu Camp
cairns.body: Barafu means ice. The camp sits on a rocky spur, and in the valley just west of it there are thick beds of sand and gravel left by vanished glaciers, with lava boulders up to three metres across balanced on the weathered sediment. Summit night starts from here around midnight.

cairns.title: The Frozen Leopard
cairns.body: In 1926 Pastor Richard Reusch — an ex-Cossack officer turned missionary who climbed this mountain forty times — found the frozen carcass of a leopard near the crater rim. Hemingway opened a story with it ten years later, noting that nobody has explained what the leopard was doing up there. The crater is named after Reusch.

cairns.title: Stella Point
cairns.body: The climb from Barafu to here is the steepest thing on the mountain: about 1,150 vertical metres in three and a half kilometres, an average grade near 28 percent, done in the dark. You reach the rim usually around dawn, with Mawenzi's jagged silhouette to the east.

cairns.title: The Vanishing Ice
cairns.body: Compare the surveys and the satellite images and roughly three quarters of the southern glacier's extent has gone in about seventy years. At that rate it disappears within a couple of decades. UNESCO expects Kilimanjaro's last glaciers to be gone by around 2050 — you are walking past something that will not be here for the next generation of climbers.

cairns.title: Uhuru Peak
cairns.body: The highest point in Africa and the highest freestanding mountain on earth, on the southern rim of Kibo's crater. Hans Meyer and Ludwig Purtscheller reached it on 6 October 1889 — and a century later the organisers of the anniversary recognised Yohani Kinyala Lauwo, the local guide who climbed with them, as a joint first-ascender. He died in 1996, 107 years after that morning. You climbed 4,255 metres from the gate to stand here.
